t: Distributed-HISQ: A Distributed Quantum Control Architecture
pb: Distributed quantum control architectures (DQCAs) for superconducting qubits face two blockers: existing lock-step synchronization schemes incur large execution overheads (idle time or full program broadcast across controllers), and existing quantum ISAs are either too high-level or too hardware-specific to support diverse qubit technologies and gate implementation strategies on a single microarchitecture.
me: Distributed-HISQ comprises two mechanisms: (1) HISQ, a hardware instruction set built as an extension to RISC-V 32I that abstracts quantum control as 'send codeword X to port Y at time T,' decoupling instruction semantics from both quantum-operation meaning and analog electronics; and (2) BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol), which exploits the deterministic duration of quantum gates to pre-book synchronization points in advance, achieving zero-cycle overhead when the deterministic tasks preceding sync are long enough to hide inter-controller communication latency. The system uses a hybrid tree+mesh network topology, with a balanced tree for region-level remote sync and mesh-like intra-layer links mirroring qubit device topology for nearest-neighbor sync. BISP hardware costs only 13 LUTs per SyncU on an FPGA.
nv: The booking-based synchronization protocol (BISP) allows controllers to pre-announce their synchronization time-points before reaching them, eliminating the round-trip latency overhead of prior on-demand sync schemes and enabling zero-cycle synchronization overhead in the common case.

mx.speedup: 22.8% reduction in average program execution time vs. lock-step baseline
mx.accuracy: ~5x reduction in infidelity vs. lock-step baseline for long-range CNOT circuits
mx.other: BISP SyncU costs only 13 LUTs; HISQ full control board: 4155 LUTs, 6392 FFs, 2.46 Mb BRAM

th: distributed quantum control architecture with zero-overhead synchronization

t: SMX: Heterogeneous Architecture for Universal Sequence Alignment Acceleration
pb: Sequence alignment accelerators are over-specialized to one alignment model (e.g., Smith-Waterman with affine gaps or simple substitution matrices) and fail to support the full variety of irregular use cases in practice (DNA, protein, ASCII text; weighted gaps; diverse substitution matrices), while general-purpose CPUs and GPUs lack the efficiency of domain-specific designs.
me: SMX is a heterogeneous architecture that integrates two components orchestrated by a general-purpose core: an ISA extension (SMX-1D) for irregular and sequential alignment tasks, and a specialized 2D coprocessor (SMX-2D) to accelerate the regular, parallel compute-intensive phases of dynamic programming. The ISA extension adds new instructions to handle variable-length sequences and edge cases, while the coprocessor accelerates the systolic-style inner-loop wavefront computation. Both components support multiple sequence types (DNA, protein, ASCII) and alignment models including weighted affine gap penalties and full substitution matrices, enabling seamless integration with state-of-the-art software alignment algorithms. Physical design targets a 22nm technology node with an area of 0.34mm², 30% of a single-issue in-order CPU core.
nv: A unified heterogeneous architecture pairing an ISA extension for irregular tasks with a dedicated 2D coprocessor for regular wavefront computation, achieving high flexibility across alignment types while delivering over 18x peak performance per area versus specialized accelerators.

mx.speedup: 256–744x over state-of-the-art software; up to 18.5x more peak performance per area vs specialized hardware accelerators
mx.area: 0.34mm² at 22nm (30% of a single-issue in-order CPU core)

th: Heterogeneous ISA+coprocessor architecture for universal sequence alignment

t: RTGS: Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM via Multi-Level Redundancy Reduction
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems cannot achieve real-time throughput (>=30 FPS) on edge devices; even the most efficient 3DGS-SLAM algorithms run at 0.78–14 FPS on a state-of-the-art edge GPU (NVIDIA ONX). The rendering and backpropagation stages dominate runtime (>80%), with severe workload imbalance across pixels and costly atomic gradient aggregation causing memory conflicts.
me: RTGS is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework targeting 3DGS-SLAM. On the algorithm side: (1) adaptive Gaussian pruning progressively removes low-importance Gaussians by reusing gradients from the backpropagation pass (no added overhead for importance scoring), and (2) dynamic downsampling reduces non-keyframe resolution from 1/16 to 1/4 of full resolution based on temporal distance to nearest keyframe, reusing keyframe identification and alpha-computing results. On the hardware side, a plug-in ASIC integrated alongside edge GPU SMs includes: (1) a Workload Scheduling Unit (WSU) combining pixel-level pairwise scheduling with subtile-level streaming, exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity to reuse scheduling patterns; (2) a Rendering & Backpropagation (R&B) Buffer that stores forward-pass intermediate values (accumulated transmittance T and per-Gaussian color contributions) to eliminate recomputation during backpropagation, reducing alpha gradient latency from 20 to 4 cycles; and (3) a Gradient Merging Unit (GMU) using a Benes network and bypass-extended reduction tree to perform pipelined sparse gradient aggregation, replacing atomic-add operations with structured in-order merging. The design is implemented at 28 nm, 500 MHz, 8.11 W, 28.41 mm2.
nv: Exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity in SLAM (where Gaussians are fixed between tracking iterations) to amortize scheduling overhead across iterations, enabling lightweight pixel-level pairwise scheduling that approaches oracle load balance with negligible cost.

mx.speedup: up to 48.8x over edge GPU baseline (ONX); real-time >=30 FPS on four datasets
mx.energy_or_tops_w: up to 82.5x energy efficiency over edge GPU baseline
mx.accuracy: ATE and PSNR within 10% variance vs. unmodified baselines
mx.other: Gradient merging latency reduced 68% vs. atomic ops; alpha gradient compute reduced from 20 to 4 cycles

th: algorithm-hardware co-design for real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM on edge

t: Accurate Leakage Speculation for Quantum Error Correction
pb: Physical qubits in quantum error correction (QEC) can leak into higher energy states (e.g., |2>), corrupting syndrome measurements and spreading errors to neighboring qubits; detecting leakage on data qubits is especially hard because they are never directly measured during QEC cycles.
me: GLADIATOR frames leakage detection as a graph labeling problem. Offline, it constructs a code-aware error-propagation graph whose nodes are syndrome patterns and weighted directed edges represent transition probabilities under leakage vs. non-leakage errors, calibrated to device characterization data. Each node accumulates incoming leakage-edge weights (W_L) and non-leakage-edge weights (W_NL); nodes where W_L > W_NL by a threshold factor are labeled as leakage patterns and compiled into a lookup table. Online, a parity-adjacency generator extracts a 5-bit syndrome pattern per data qubit each QEC cycle and a combinational sequence checker (at most 10 LUTs per data qubit) classifies it in under 1 ns, triggering an LRC only for patterns flagged as leakage-dominated. GLADIATOR-D extends the design to a two-round sliding window of syndrome history for further accuracy. The method generalizes to surface codes, color codes, and qLDPC codes.
nv: A probabilistic graph-labeling framework that distinguishes leakage-induced syndrome patterns from standard Pauli-error patterns using calibrated transition probabilities, enabling code-agnostic, low-overhead leakage speculation that requires at most 10 LUTs per data qubit versus 177-5393 LUTs for prior work.

mx.speedup: 1.7x-3.9x QEC cycle speedup vs. always-LRC baseline
mx.area: <0.1% LUTs at code distance 25 on Kintex UltraScale+ FPGA; 10 LUTs per data qubit
mx.accuracy: 16% reduction in logical error rate; 1.91x lower false-positive rate vs. eraser
mx.other: 17x-63x FPGA LUT reduction vs. eraser across code distances 5-25; combinational logic evaluates in <1 ns

th: accurate leakage speculation for quantum error correction

t: Flexing RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors to Extreme Edge
pb: Extreme edge applications (smart labels, wearable healthcare, smart textiles) require processors that are ultra-low area, ultra-low power, conformable, and low-cost—properties that conventional silicon RISC-V processors and existing smallest designs like Serv cannot meet—while still supporting programmability for occasional firmware updates.
me: The paper proposes RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors (RISSPs), generated by an automated methodology that (1) compiles applications to the full RV32E ISA to identify the required instruction subset (typically 24-86% of the ISA), (2) pulls formally pre-verified instruction hardware blocks from a library where each RISC-V instruction is implemented as a standalone, fully verified RTL block, (3) stitches them into a Modular Execution Unit (ModularEX) via a case-statement switch, and (4) synthesizes the result with commercial EDA tools (Synopsys ICC2 or Cadence Innovus) on Pragmatic Semiconductor's 0.6-um IGZO FlexIC process, where synthesis tools automatically eliminate redundant gates. A single-cycle non-pipelined microarchitecture suffices for kHz-range extreme edge performance requirements. For long-lasting applications needing firmware updates, a generative AI tool rewrites instructions not in the subset using equivalent subset instructions.
nv: A bottom-up RISSP generation methodology built on a library of formally pre-verified instruction-granularity RTL blocks, enabling automated generation of minimal-area FlexIC processors without conventional design-and-verify cycles for each new application.

mx.energy_or_tops_w: ~40x more energy-efficient per instruction than Serv
mx.area: 8-43% area reduction vs. full RV32E processor (synthesis); up to 42% reduction in FlexIC physical implementation
mx.ppa: 3-30% power reduction vs. full RISC-V; up to 21% in physical FlexIC; max frequency 1500-1850 kHz on 0.6-um IGZO process
mx.other: Applications use only 24-86% of full RV32E ISA (9-32 distinct instructions at -O2)

th: automated RISC-V instruction-subset processor generation for flexible extreme-edge electronics

t: REACT3D: Real-time Edge Accelerator for Incremental Training in 3D Gaussian Splatting based SLAM Systems
pb: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM requires incremental training and rendering at over 30 FPS on edge devices, but existing GPU-based solutions and prior accelerators fall short due to redundant training computation, unnecessary loss computation, and irregular memory access patterns. The combination of continuous camera streaming, per-Gaussian gradient accumulation, and sparse activated Gaussian sets creates severe compute and memory irregularity.
me: REACT3D introduces two algorithmic optimizations: (1) spatial consistency and convergence-aware sparsification that predicts under-optimized Gaussians based on spatial coherence and convergence dynamics, eliminating redundant forward/backward rendering passes; and (2) a pixel block-wise fine-grained dataflow that fuses loss computation into the rendering pipeline, removing explicit loss storage. At the architectural level, a Content Addressable Memory (CAM)-based Dual-index Gaussian Buffer resolves discontinuous memory accesses by maintaining two parallel indices into the Gaussian buffer, avoiding computation conflicts during gradient merging across scattered Gaussian-to-pixel mappings.
nv: The CAM-based Dual-index Gaussian Buffer that resolves the irregular memory access and gradient-merging conflict problem inherent to 3DGS training on sparse, streaming SLAM data.

mx.energy_or_tops_w: 33.69x energy efficiency improvement over NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin
mx.other: Achieves >30 FPS real-time 3DGS SLAM threshold

th: Real-time 3DGS SLAM edge acceleration

t: Towards Closing the Performance Gap for Cryptographic Kernels Between CPUs and Specialized Hardware
pb: Achieving near-ASIC performance for cryptographic kernels (Number Theoretic Transform, NTT; and large-integer BLAS operations) on commodity x86 CPUs remains an open challenge; current CPU baselines lag ASICs by orders of magnitude for these workloads, which are foundational to post-quantum cryptography and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE).
me: The paper develops optimized scalar x86-64 implementations of NTT and large-integer BLAS at the per-core level, then applies SIMD vectorization using AVX2 and AVX-512 to achieve 38x and 62x speedup over state-of-the-art CPU baselines for NTT and BLAS respectively. To narrow the remaining gap, the authors propose a small x86 ISA extension called MQX (multi-word extension) that adds three new instructions targeting multi-precision modular arithmetic patterns common in NTT and BLAS. MQX cuts the slowdown relative to ASICs to as low as 35x per core; a roofline analysis of multi-core scaling shows that top-tier server CPUs with MQX can approach ASIC-level throughput.
nv: The MQX (multi-word extension) ISA extension — just three new AVX-512 instructions targeting multi-precision modular arithmetic — that closes much of the remaining gap between x86 CPUs and cryptographic ASICs for NTT and large-integer BLAS.

mx.speedup: 38x over CPU baseline for NTT; 62x for BLAS (with AVX-512); ASIC slowdown reduced to 35x per core with MQX

th: Closing CPU-to-ASIC performance gap for cryptographic kernels via SIMD and minimal ISA extension

t: FedProphet: Memory-Efficient Federated Adversarial Training via Robust and Consistent Cascade Learning
pb: Federated Adversarial Training (FAT) requires large models to attain high accuracy and robustness, but memory-constrained edge devices cannot fit full-model training; existing memory-efficient FL methods sacrifice accuracy or robustness through objective inconsistency between local and global models.
me: FedProphet uses adversarial cascade learning: the full model is split into small sequential modules, each trained on one class of devices. Strong convexity regularization on each module's loss ensures local module objectives remain consistent with the global adversarial loss. A server-side coordinator performs Adaptive Perturbation Adjustment (APA) to balance utility vs. robustness trade-off dynamically, and Differentiated Module Assignment (DMA) to assign modules to heterogeneous devices, mitigating objective inconsistency across rounds.
nv: Cascade learning with strong convexity regularization that simultaneously achieves memory efficiency and adversarial robustness in federated settings, proven to imply low objective inconsistency, combined with APA and DMA coordinators on the server.
hw: Memory-constrained edge devices (federated); server-side coordination node
wl: Federated adversarial training on image classification (CIFAR-10, Caltech-256)
th: Training Efficiency & Memory

t: VoLUT: Efficient Volumetric streaming enhanced by LUT-based super-resolution
pb: 3D volumetric video streaming requires extremely high bandwidth; downsampling before transmission and upsampling via super-resolution at the receiver is needed, but existing 3D SR algorithms are too slow for real-time use on commodity mobile devices.
me: VoLUT has a two-stage SR pipeline. Stage 1 (dilated kNN interpolation): broader spatial context via dilated k-nearest neighbor search for initial upsampling; octree parallelism accelerates the kNN computation; neighbor relationships are reused across upsampling steps. Stage 2 (LUT refinement): coordinates of upsampled points are normalized to [0,1], quantized into b discrete bins per axis (bin=128 by default), and looked up in a precomputed 3D LUT that stores high-resolution position offsets (RF=4 receptive field, bin=128 yields 1.6GB LUT). The LUT is built offline from a trained NN model. MPC (Model Predictive Control)-based adaptive bitrate algorithm dynamically selects downsampling rate based on network conditions, streaming a continuous range of quality levels.
nv: First system to run high-quality 3D point cloud super-resolution on commodity mobile devices at line-rate, using offline NN-to-LUT conversion with position encoding quantization and dilated kNN interpolation, combined with MPC-based continuous ABR streaming.
hw: Commodity mobile devices (receiver-side); server-side encoding; edge streaming
th: Efficient Inference on Edge/Mobile
